 Diwali, also known as Deepawali, is one of the most widely celebrated Hindu festivals in India. The festival is traditionally associated with the triumph of light over darkness and good over evil. While Diwali is commonly described as a five-day celebration beginning with Dhanteras and ending with Bhai Dooj, festivities in different parts of the country follow regional calendars and customs.
 In 2026, the Deepawali celebrations listed in the calendar begin on November 5 with Govatsa Dwadashi and conclude on November 11 with Bhai Dooj. The main Lakshmi Puja and Diwali celebrations are scheduled for November 8.

 Across these days, families observe traditional rituals, decorate their homes with diyas and rangoli, exchange gifts and worship different deities. Goddess Lakshmi, the deity associated with wealth and prosperity, holds particular importance during Diwali.
 Diwali 2026: Full 7-Day Calendar and Festival Dates 
 Here is the day-wise schedule of Deepawali 2026, including the dates, tithis and major observances. 
 Date Day Festival and Observances 
 November 5, 2026 Thursday Govatsa Dwadashi, Vasu Baras 
 November 6, 2026 Friday Dhanteras, Dhantrayodashi, Dhanvantari Trayodashi, Yama Deepam 
 November 7, 2026 Saturday Kali Chaudas, Hanuman Puja 
 November 8, 2026 Sunday Narak Chaturdashi, Tamil Deepavali, Lakshmi Puja, Diwali, Kali Puja, Chopda Puja, Sharda Puja 
 November 9, 2026 Monday Diwali Snan, Diwali Devpuja 
 November 10, 2026 Tuesday Govardhan Puja, Annakut, Bali Pratipada, Gujarati New Year 
 November 11, 2026 Wednesday Bhai Dooj, Bhau Beej, Yama Dwitiya, Chitragupta Puja 
 Diwali 2026: Significance of Each Day 
 November 5: Govatsa Dwadashi

 The festivities begin with Govatsa Dwadashi, also known as Vasu Baras in Maharashtra. The day is associated with the worship of cows and their calves, which hold a special place in Hindu traditions. Devotees offer prayers and express gratitude for their importance in agricultural and domestic life.

 November 6: Dhanteras 
 Dhanteras, also known as Dhantrayodashi, marks an important day in the Diwali celebrations. People traditionally buy gold, silver, utensils and other valuables, considering the occasion auspicious for new purchases. Goddess Lakshmi and Lord Dhanvantari are worshipped for prosperity and good health. Yama Deepam, the ritual of lighting a lamp in honour of Yama, the god of death, is also observed in several regions.

 November 7: Kali Chaudas 
 Kali Chaudas is observed on the day before the main Diwali celebrations in some regional traditions. Also known as Narak Chaturdashi in certain calendars, the day is associated with prayers to Goddess Kali and Lord Hanuman. Devotees perform rituals seeking protection and the removal of negativity.
 November 8: Narak Chaturdashi and Lakshmi Puja 
 November 8 marks the main Diwali celebrations in the calendar, along with Narak Chaturdashi and Tamil Deepavali. Families decorate their homes with lamps, flowers and rangoli, while evening prayers are offered to Goddess Lakshmi and Lord Ganesha.
 Lakshmi Puja is one of the most significant rituals of Diwali. Goddess Lakshmi is worshipped for wealth, prosperity and well-being, while Lord Ganesha is invoked for wisdom and the removal of obstacles. Kali Puja is also observed in several parts of the country, particularly in Bengal.
 The day also holds importance for traders and business communities, who perform Chopda Puja and Sharda Puja as part of their traditional observances.
 November 9: Diwali Snan and Devpuja 
 The day following the main Diwali observance is marked by Diwali Snan and Devpuja in the calendar. Devotees follow customary bathing and worship rituals, with practices varying across regions and communities.
 November 10: Govardhan Puja 
 Govardhan Puja, also known as Annakut, is celebrated a day after Diwali in many parts of India. The festival commemorates Lord Krishna's protection of the people of Vrindavan by lifting Govardhan Hill. Devotees prepare a variety of food offerings, arrange them as Annakut and offer prayers to Lord Krishna. The day is also observed as Bali Pratipada in several traditions and marks the Gujarati New Year.
 November 11: Bhai Dooj 
 The five-day Diwali festivities traditionally conclude with Bhai Dooj, also known as Bhau Beej and Yama Dwitiya. The festival celebrates the bond between brothers and sisters. Sisters apply a tilak on their brothers' foreheads and pray for their long lives and well-being, while brothers offer gifts and reaffirm their affection and support.
 Why is Goddess Lakshmi worshipped during Diwali? 
 Goddess Lakshmi is regarded as the deity of wealth, prosperity and abundance. Her worship is central to Diwali celebrations, particularly on Amavasya, the new Moon day associated with Lakshmi Puja. Families clean and decorate their homes before the festival, light diyas and offer prayers to welcome prosperity and good fortune. Lord Ganesha is worshipped alongside Goddess Lakshmi, with devotees seeking wisdom, success and the removal of obstacles.
 Diwali Puja is not limited to homes. Traditional business communities also perform prayers at their workplaces and shops. Traders worship their account books, pens and inkpots as part of the ritual. These objects are traditionally associated with Goddess Saraswati and Goddess Maha Kali, reflecting the importance of knowledge, record-keeping and business practices.
 Diwali Lakshmi Puja 2026: Why is Pradosh muhurat important? 
 The timing of Lakshmi Puja is considered significant in Hindu traditions. The preferred period for Diwali worship is after sunset, during Pradosh Kaal. The Diwali date is determined by the Amavasya Tithi prevailing during this period.
 Pradosh begins after sunset and is considered an auspicious time for evening worship. Even if the Amavasya period overlaps with Pradosh for only a short duration, the corresponding Puja Muhurat is traditionally considered important. Since festival dates and rituals can differ across regions, devotees should consult their local panchang for the precise Diwali Puja Muhurat and other observances.
